subagent_reports.topic: Test-only design for fixing CI-flaky latency benchmarks (aggregation semantics)

sources.label: CPython statistics.median source + docs
sources.summary: median(data) sorts and returns middle value; for even count returns mean of the two middle values (n//2-1, n//2). Robust central location; less affected by outliers. No NaN handling. Raises StatisticsError on empty.

sources.label: CPython statistics.quantiles docs
sources.summary: quantiles(data, n=100, method='inclusive'|'exclusive'). inclusive: i-th sorted point maps to quantile (i-1)/(m-1); exclusive: i/(m+1), both linear-interpolate. Docs warn 'For meaningful results, number of data points should exceed n' — with n=100 and only 10 samples, p95 is ill-defined/coarse.

sources.label: lgrep pyproject.toml
sources.summary: requires-python = '>=3.11'. statistics.quantiles (added 3.8) and median are guaranteed available. No statistics.trimmed_mean exists in stdlib (confirmed via docs inventory: mean/fmean/median/median_low/median_high/harmonic_mean/mode/quantiles/stdev/variance — no trimmed mean).

sources.label: Current test file
sources.summary: Lines 96-97 and 162-163: p95 = latencies[int(len(latencies)*0.95)] on 10 sorted samples = latencies[9] = the MAX, mislabeled as p95. Budgets: SEMANTIC_SEARCH_P95_BUDGET_MS=100.0, SYMBOL_SEARCH_P95_BUDGET_MS=50.0, INDEX_FOLDER_BUDGET_MS=5000.0. n=10 queries each.

sources.label: Verified aggregation math (JS mirror of Python semantics)
sources.summary: CI scenario [0.3,0.4,0.25,0.5,0.35,0.45,0.3,0.4,0.35,159.0]: median=0.375, inclusive_p95=87.675, exclusive_p95=159.0 (extrapolates to outlier), old_idx_'p95'=159.0(=max). Uniform regression [30]*10: median=30.05. Healthy sample median=0.29.

subagent_reports.architecture_assessment: The aggregation is fundamentally wrong: latencies[int(len(latencies)*0.95)] on 10 samples is index 9 = the max, so the test asserts 'max < budget' while calling it p95. Max has a 0% breakdown point — any single scheduler stall fails it (exactly the two CI failures). No percentile computed from 10 samples is robust: inclusive p95 still interpolates toward the max (verified 87.7ms > 50ms budget for the CI scenario), and exclusive p95 extrapolates BEYOND the max to the outlier value (159ms). The math-only correction (compute a real p95) does NOT fix flakiness — confirming the task's proven fact. The structurally correct fix is to aggregate central tendency with the maximum breakdown point: statistics.median. Median of 10 = mean of 5th and 6th sorted values, so a single outlier (top half) has zero effect; it requires 6+ of 10 samples to move (50% breakdown point). A uniform code regression moves every sample, so the median moves with it and trips the budget. This separates '1/10 slow' (scheduler noise, ignore) from '10/10 slow' (real regression, catch). median is a single stdlib call with no index arithmetic, eliminating the off-by-one class that caused the original bug.

validation.notes: Recommended design (statistics.median, keep n=10, keep budgets, optional high hang-ceiling) is test-only, deterministic, retains regression coverage, and is backed by stdlib docs + verified numeric evidence. No blockers.

tradeoffs: Median ignores the entire top half: a regression affecting <=5 of 10 samples is masked. For a uniform code-path regression (affects 100% of queries) this never occurs, so coverage of the intended regression class is preserved.
Lower statistical efficiency than mean in clean data — irrelevant here given ~100-200x budget margin (median ~0.3ms vs 50/100ms budgets).
Switching max->median changes the asserted statistic; any future tail-latency SLA would need dedicated profiling, not this CI unit test.
A per-sample ceiling at the regression budget (current behavior) remains flaky; only a much higher hang-ceiling (e.g. 1000ms) is non-flaky and must be framed as a deadlock guard, not a latency guard.

alternatives_considered.option: trimmed mean (drop min+max, average middle 8): statistics.mean(sorted(latencies)[1:-1])
alternatives_considered.rationale: Works numerically (verified 0.381ms on CI scenario) but (a) stdlib has no trimmed_mean so it requires manual slicing, reintroducing the exact index-arithmetic/off-by-one class that caused the original bug; (b) lower breakdown point (~10-20%, tolerates only 1 outlier in 10) vs median's 50%. Median is strictly more robust AND simpler.

Docs warn 'data points should exceed n' for meaningful results; with 10 samples p95 is ill-defined and dominated by the max. Verified inclusive p95 of the CI scenario = 87.7ms, still > 50ms budget — does not fix flakiness. Exclusive method extrapolates to the outlier (159ms), worse. Percentiles need ~40+ samples (4x test cost) to be robust; over-engineering here.
Explicitly disallowed by task. Also ineffective: scheduler stalls are unbounded; any budget that survives a 159ms stall is meaningless as a latency guard.

alternatives_considered.option: increase sample count to 40+ to make p95 meaningful
alternatives_considered.rationale: Would 4x test cost for no benefit over median. Median at n=10 already achieves 50% breakdown point with the existing cost. Violates simplicity.

architecture_judgement.recommendation: Adopt statistics.median as the aggregator; keep n=10 and existing budgets; add optional 1000ms hang-ceiling as a separate deadlock guard. Add parametrized pure unit tests of the aggregator proving (1) one 159ms outlier ignored, (2) uniform above-budget regression caught, (3) healthy passes, (4) even-count mean-of-middle-two interpolation, (5) boundary strictness (< vs <=).

subagent_reports.recommendation: RECOMMENDATION FOR ORCHESTRATOR: 1) Replace latencies[int(len(latencies)*0.95)] with statistics.median(latencies) in BOTH test methods (lines ~97 and ~163); add `import statistics`. 2) Keep n=10 queries (no cost change; median needs no more samples). 3) Keep budgets 100.0/50.0/5000.0 ms (they give ~100-200x margin over steady-state median ~0.3ms, which is what makes the assertion stable). 4) RENAME the asserted variable/labels from 'p95' to 'median' in messages, budget constant names, and docstrings to stop the mislabeling (the budget names say P95 — update to MEDIAN to match the statistic). 5) Optionally add `assert max(latencies) < 1000.0` as a separate 'hang/deadlock guard' (NOT at the 50/100ms regression budget — that reintroduces flakiness). 6) Add a parametrized unit test for the aggregation helper covering the 5 cases in the test plan. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: semantic median < 100.0ms; symbol median < 50.0ms; (optional) every sample < 1000ms hang guard. Regression-coverage preserved: a uniform regression pushing all samples above budget still fails (median moves with the distribution).
follow_ups: When budget constant names are renamed from P95 to MEDIAN, also update the module docstring lines 10-11 ('asserts p95 latency') to match, or reviewers will re-flag the mislabel.
If a real tail-latency (p95/p99) SLA becomes a product requirement later, add a dedicated profiling benchmark with n>=40 — do not retrofit percentiles onto this 10-sample CI unit test.
The optional 1000ms hang-ceiling should be tuned against future CI if any stall is observed near it; 159ms observed gives ~6x margin but is based on only 2 data points.

subagent_reports.topic: Design validation - flaky latency benchmark median fix

sources.label: Repo: actual flaky test file
sources.summary: Current 'p95' is int(9.5)=9 -> the max of 10 sorted samples. One scheduler stall (outlier) decides CI. This is the confirmed flakiness root cause.

sources.label: Repo: Python version requirements
sources.locator: pyproject.toml (requires-python >=3.11; classifiers 3.11/3.12/3.13; tool.ruff target-version py311; asyncio_mode auto)
sources.summary: Project requires Python 3.11+; statistics.median (stdlib since 3.4) is guaranteed available on all CI matrix versions. Constraint C4 satisfied. Pure tests use stdlib only.

sources.label: Python stdlib docs: statistics.median
sources.summary: median sorts then averages the two middle order statistics for even n. No percentile-index arithmetic to get wrong. Correct robust estimator for n=10.

sources.label: Repo: related-scan grep for sibling defects
sources.locator: grep across tests/ for 'len(latencies)*0.95|p95|percentile|int(len' -> only test_benchmark_latency.py
sources.summary: No sibling tests use the broken truncated-index pattern. Design scope (single file) is complete; no related-scan follow-up required.

sources.label: IEEE-754 / CPython float behavior
sources.summary: AC2 inputs 0.35/0.4 are not exactly representable; CPython statistics.median computes (data[i-1]+data[i])/2. Exact-equality assertion on the 0.375 result is fragile; tolerance (pytest.approx) is the robust assertion style.

subagent_reports.architecture_assessment: The design correctly replaces a hand-rolled pseudo-percentile that is actually the max (int(len*0.95)==latencies[9] for n=10) with statistics.median, a stdlib robust estimator with a 50% breakdown point. The defect root cause is confirmed against the real code: a single shared-runner scheduler stall becomes the max and fails CI, exactly the reported flakiness. Median over n=10 ignores up to 4 high outliers (the 5th breaks it = 50% breakdown), so one stall cannot decide the result, while a uniform regression shifts every sample and still trips the existing 50ms/100ms budgets (AC3). The separate 1000ms-per-sample hang guard is a thoughtful compensating control: switching from max to median loses single-outlier detection, and the guard restores catastrophic/hang detection without re-flagging ordinary outliers. Constraints are respected: test-only (C1), 10 calls retained (C2), budgets unchanged 100/50 with no skip/inflate (C3), stdlib median on 3.11+ (C4). All six ACs are addressable by the planned test set and the arithmetic is verified. Deviation vs the by-the-book robust-statistics approach: NONE. The honest scoping (tail-latency SLA is out of scope, OOS1) is appropriate for a shared-runner unit test.

validation.notes: Design is sound and minimal (P19). Three implementer-level cautions do not block the design gate: (1) AC2's 0.375 derives from non-exactly-representable inputs 0.35/0.4 - implementer MUST assert via pytest.approx/tolerance, not exact ==, to avoid reintroducing equality fragility; (2) the AC5 1000ms hang guard is a runtime inline assertion with no pure boundary test (recommend adding 999.x passes / 1000.0 fails strict); (3) design prose 'withstands five outliers at n=10' is imprecise - median withstands 4, breaks at the 5th (50% breakdown point); one-word doc fix. Conscious tradeoff accepted: single-sample regressions in [budget,1000ms) now pass undetected (documented as OOS1).

tradeoffs: Median robustness vs single-sample tail sensitivity: a partial regression affecting <50% of calls in [budget,1000ms) is no longer caught (consciously accepted, OOS1; hang guard preserves catastrophic detection).
Float-equality assertion style: AC2 expected value must use pytest.approx; exact == risks a NEW equality-flakiness class that ironically defeats the fix's purpose.

Detection gap between budget (50/100ms) and hang guard (1000ms): the old max-based test incidentally caught any single outlier above budget; the new design deliberately does not for non-hang outliers.

alternatives_considered.rationale: Not statistically meaningful at n=10; even inclusive p95 still tracks the isolated outlier and reproduces the flakiness. Design rejection is correct.
Mean has 0 breakdown point - one outlier dominates. Would not fix the flakiness; median is strictly better for this signal. (Evaluated here; not in design's list.)
Hand-rolled slice arithmetic reopens the same defect class (off-by-one index selection). Median avoids the arithmetic entirely.
Median is already robust at n=10; increasing samples violates C2 (suite-runtime increase) for no robustness gain.
Violates C3 and masks the problem, weakening regression coverage. Budgets must stay at existing 100/50.

architecture_judgement.recommendation: Proceed with the design as written. Engineering execution must: (1) use pytest.approx/tolerance for the AC2 0.375 median-value assertion; (2) add a pure boundary test for the AC5 hang guard (e.g. 999.9ms passes, 1000.0ms fails strict <); (3) correct the 'withstands five outliers' prose to 'withstands four, breaks at five (50% breakdown point)'. No design-gate blocker.

subagent_reports.recommendation: PASS. The design correctly fixes the confirmed root cause (broken pseudo-p95 == max) with stdlib statistics.median, honors all constraints C1-C4, and all six ACs are covered by the planned pure + runtime tests with verified arithmetic. Proceed to planning/execution with the three implementer cautions above (float tolerance on AC2; pure hang-guard boundary test; breakdown-point prose fix).

documents.proposal:
# Fix flaky latency benchmarks

## Why

Both latency benchmarks assert on the maximum of ten samples while calling it p95. A single scheduling stall on a shared CI runner fails them. This has taken trunk red twice within one hour — PR #6 job 90779400278, then main run 30517051431 — and will keep doing so intermittently.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Symptom.** `tests/test_benchmark_latency.py::TestSymbolSearchLatency::test_search_symbols_latency` fails on CI with `Symbol search p95 latency 109.2ms exceeds budget 50.0ms`, while nine of its ten samples were under 2ms.

**Immediate cause.** Both benchmarks compute the percentile the same way, at `tests/test_benchmark_latency.py:97` and `:163`:

```python
latencies.sort()
p95 = latencies[int(len(latencies) * 0.95)]
```

For `len == 10`, `int(0.95 * 10)` is `int(9.5)` = `9`. `latencies[9]` is the last element of a sorted ten-element list — the maximum. The docstring at line 33, the variable name, and the assertion messages at lines 100 and 166 all claim p95. The assertion is on max.

**Root cause.** Two independent faults compound, and fixing either alone leaves the test flaky.

1. *The statistic is maximally outlier-sensitive.* Index selection by truncation collapses to the maximum at n=10. A percentile is chosen to be robust to tail outliers; taking the max is the opposite of that intent. Nothing in the test can distinguish a genuine regression from one unlucky sample.

2. *The sample size cannot support a tail statistic.* Even with correct arithmetic, ten samples cannot estimate a 95th percentile robustly — the top one or two values dominate any method. Verified: a true inclusive p95 over the trunk failure's samples is 60.8ms, still above the 50ms budget. Over the PR #6 samples it is 139.1ms. So the percentile bug is real, but repairing it is insufficient.

Underneath both: the benchmark measures an operation of roughly 0.3ms against a 50ms wall-clock budget on a shared runner. Reproduced locally over twelve consecutive calls: 0.19ms to 0.55ms, no first-call penalty (`index_folder` warms the shared index cache in-process, so cold-start is not the explanation). The signal is three orders of magnitude smaller than the noise floor of a contended CI runner, so any single-sample-sensitive assertion is flaky by construction regardless of how generous the budget looks.

**Why it was not caught.** The tests pass on an idle machine and on most CI runs, so the defect only surfaces under contention. Nothing asserts a property of the measurement method itself, so a statistic that cannot fail correctly still looks like passing coverage. The 150x apparent margin actively disguised the problem: a budget that generous reads as obviously safe.

## What Changes

1. Replace the truncated-index selection with a real percentile, and raise the sample count so a tail statistic is meaningful. At roughly 0.3ms per call, 100 samples remain well under a second.
2. Alternatively or additionally, assert a robust central statistic (median or trimmed mean) as the regression signal, with a separate deliberately generous ceiling for pathological cases. A regression in the operation moves the median; a runner stall does not.
3. Apply the same correction to the semantic-search benchmark at line 97, which carries the identical defect.
4. Make the naming honest — whatever statistic is asserted should be what the variable, docstring, and failure message say.
5. Keep a meaningful regression budget. Raising the threshold until it stops failing is explicitly rejected: it would preserve the mislabeled statistic and weaken the only latency coverage in the suite.

## User Outcomes

- [ ] Trunk CI stops failing intermittently on unrelated changes
- [ ] A genuine latency regression is still caught
- [ ] A single CI scheduling stall no longer fails the build
- [ ] The reported statistic is the statistic actually asserted
- [ ] Discovery will firm acceptance criteria and success criteria

## Affected Code

- `tests/test_benchmark_latency.py` — both `test_search_semantic_local_latency` (line 97) and `test_search_symbols_latency` (line 163); percentile computation, sample count, budget constants, docstrings, and assertion messages

## Constraints

- Test-only change; do not modify `src/lgrep/` behavior.
- Keep total suite runtime increase negligible.
- Do not delete or skip the benchmarks; regression coverage must survive.
- Do not simply raise the budget to mask the flakiness.

## Impact

CI reliability only. No user-facing or runtime behavior changes.

## Risks

- A more robust statistic could mask a real regression that only affects tail latency. Mitigated by retaining a separate ceiling assertion so pathological outliers are still visible.
- Raising the sample count slightly increases suite runtime; bounded by the sub-millisecond per-call cost.

## Validation Plan

- Reproduce the defect first: assert that the current selection returns the maximum for a synthetic ten-sample list, establishing the bug as a failing test.
- Green: the corrected statistic ignores a single injected outlier while still failing on a uniformly slow distribution.
- Confirm both benchmarks are covered.
- Full suite plus `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`.
- Confirm trunk CI green after merge, across all three Python matrix versions.

Both latency benchmarks assert on the maximum of ten samples while calling it p95, which makes them fail whenever a shared CI runner stalls once. This has taken trunk red twice in one hour.

`tests/test_benchmark_latency.py:97` and `:163` both compute:

```python
latencies.sort()
p95 = latencies[int(len(latencies) * 0.95)]
```

With ten samples, `int(0.95 * 10)` is `int(9.5)` = `9`, and `latencies[9]` is the largest element of a sorted ten-element list. The docstrings, the variable name, and the assertion messages all say p95; the value is the maximum.

The operation being measured takes roughly 0.3ms. Measured locally across twelve consecutive calls: 0.19ms to 0.55ms, with no first-call penalty, because `index_folder` already warms the shared index cache in-process. The budget is 50ms — a margin of over 150x.

It still fails, because a single scheduling stall on a shared runner is enough:

| Run | Samples (ms) | Asserted value |
|---|---|---|
| main @216acba | 0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.6, 0.6, 0.9, 1.6, **109.2** | 109.2 |
| PR #6 | 0.4, 0.5, 0.5, 1.1, 47.3, 48.7, 91.6, 93.8, 114.4, **159.3** | 159.3 |

Nine of ten samples in the trunk failure were under 2ms. One stall decided the result. Correcting only the percentile arithmetic does not fix this: a true inclusive p95 over those same ten samples is 60.8ms, still above the 50ms budget.

# Agreement — Fix flaky latency benchmarks

## Objective

Restore stable green CI while preserving meaningful latency-regression coverage for local semantic and symbol search.

## Acceptance criteria

- **AC1 — Honest aggregation:** both latency benchmarks use `statistics.median` over exactly 10 measured calls. No truncated index selection, percentile claim, or max-based variable/message remains.
- **AC2 — One outlier does not decide CI:** a pure aggregation test over `[0.25, 0.3, 0.3, 0.35, 0.35, 0.4, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5, 159.0]` returns median `0.375`ms and satisfies the 50ms symbol-search budget.
- **AC3 — Uniform regression still fails:** a pure aggregation test over ten `60.0`ms samples returns median `60.0`ms and fails the 50ms symbol-search budget.
- **AC4 — Both paths covered:** semantic search keeps a strict median budget under 100ms; symbol search keeps a strict median budget under 50ms. The two existing runtime benchmarks each use the same aggregation helper.
- **AC5 — Hang guard:** every individual measured call remains below 1000ms. This is explicitly a hang/deadlock guard, not tail-latency coverage.
- **AC6 — CI recovery:** the full test suite, ruff check, and ruff format check pass locally; after merge the GitHub CI matrix passes on Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13.

## Constraints

- Test-only change: do not modify `src/lgrep/` behavior.
- Keep 10 measured calls per benchmark; no suite-runtime increase for a larger sample set.
- Do not delete, skip, or budget-inflate either benchmark.
- Use Python standard library only; project requires Python 3.11+.

## Out of scope

- A tail-latency SLA. That needs dedicated profiling/load tooling, not a shared-runner unit test.
- Changing CI runners or job topology.
- Altering the measured search implementations.
documents.design:
# Design — Fix flaky latency benchmarks

## Decision

Replace the hand-rolled pseudo-percentile with a tiny pure helper based on `statistics.median`. Both runtime benchmarks call it for their ten measured samples.

Median is the correct signal for this test:

- It withstands up to four high outliers in ten samples; the fifth can change the result.
- A uniform regression affects every query and shifts the median, so the existing 50ms symbol and 100ms semantic budgets remain meaningful.
- `statistics.median` has no percentile-index arithmetic to get wrong and is guaranteed by Python 3.11+.

## Shape

`tests/test_benchmark_latency.py` gains a private `_median_latency_ms(samples)` helper and pure unit tests for that helper. The two runtime benchmarks retain exactly ten calls, then assert:

1. median is below the existing path-specific regression budget;
2. every sample is below 1000ms, explicitly named as a hang/deadlock guard.

The assertion text and docstrings say "median," not p95. The 1000ms guard is deliberately not a tail-latency promise; it detects pathological blocking while the median detects a regression in the search path.

## Tests

- One 159ms outlier among nine sub-millisecond samples yields the expected median (`pytest.approx(0.375)`) and passes the 50ms budget.
- Ten 60ms samples yield 60ms and fail the symbol budget.
- Even-count behavior is asserted (`[1..9,100]` → 5.5) so the estimator is explicit.
- Exact-budget boundary fails because runtime assertions remain strict `<`.
- Hang guard boundary is pure-tested: 999.9ms passes, 1000.0ms fails.
- Both runtime paths use the same helper.

## Rejected alternatives

- Real p95: not statistically meaningful at n=10; even inclusive p95 still follows an isolated outlier.
- More samples: unnecessary for median and needlessly increases suite work.
- Trimmed mean: hand-rolled slice arithmetic reopens the defect class.
- Raising the budget or skipping the test: masks the problem and weakens regression coverage.

## Risk

Median does not represent a tail SLA. That is intentional; a shared-runner unit test cannot prove one. The separate hang guard preserves bounded failure detection.
documents.executiveSummary:
# Executive Summary — Fix flaky latency benchmarks

## Outcome

CI no longer lets one scheduler pause masquerade as a product regression. The two latency tests had calculated `int(10 * 0.95)`, which selected the maximum sample while claiming to report p95. One 109ms or 159ms shared-runner stall could red-line a search operation whose normal time is roughly 0.3ms.

Both benchmarks now use Python's standard `statistics.median` across the existing ten calls. The actual regression budgets remain strict: 100ms for local semantic search and 50ms for symbol search. A separate strict 1000ms per-call check catches hangs and deadlocks without pretending to be tail-latency coverage.

## Value

Unrelated changes stop failing CI because another process briefly received CPU time. At the same time, a uniform slowdown still fails: ten 60ms symbol-search samples produce a 60ms median and breach the unchanged 50ms budget.

## Verification

- Pure tests prove one 159ms outlier is ignored, uniform slow behavior fails, even-count median behavior is correct, both budgets have strict boundaries, and the hang guard is strict.
- Focused suite: 9 passed.
- Independent verification: 724 full-suite tests passed; lint and formatting clean.
- Review found and fixed missing pure boundary coverage for the semantic 100ms budget.

## Risk

This is intentionally not a tail-latency SLA; shared-runner unit tests cannot establish one. The hang guard still catches pathological blocking. Post-merge CI across Python 3.11/3.12/3.13 is release evidence.
